reasons.reason: Adiabatic means no heat flows in or out of the gas, and with nothing exchanged with the surroundings I don't see what would shift its thermal state, so the temperature stays where it started.
Compressing the gas means work is done on it, and since an adiabatic process lets no heat escape, all of that work goes into internal energy, which I'd expect to show up as a higher temperature.
Over a full cycle the system returns to its starting state, so its internal energy change is zero, and the first law then tells me the net heat added must equal the net work done.
In a cycle the heat I put in has to pay for the work done on expansion and also for an equal amount spent bringing the system back, so the total heat comes to twice W.
A parabola is symmetric about its axis, so parallel rays striking opposite sides reflect inward and meet in the middle of the curve, which puts the focus at the center of the shape.
A parabola is built around its focus, a point on the axis at a set distance from the vertex, and every ray arriving parallel to the axis reflects through that one point.

The middle lamella runs between the outer cells as a continuous pectin layer, so its main structural job, as I read it, is sealing the tissue and stopping water from escaping through the leaf surface.
Homogalacturonan has stretches of de-esterified carboxyl groups that bind calcium into an egg-box gel, and that gel is what glues neighbouring cells together and sets how porous the wall is.

Epithermal gold forms where hot fluids boil close to the surface, and bladed calcite in quartz veins records exactly that boiling, so I'd treat it as the mark of the hydrothermal system carrying the gold.

High-sulfidation fluids are strongly acidic from magmatic sulfur gases, and that acid leaches rock into vuggy silica while forming alunite and kaolinite, so I'd read advanced argillic alteration as the system's signature.
Kepler's third law says the period squared equals the semi-major axis cubed, so for 4 AU I cube it to get 64, and the square root of 64 gives a period of 8 years.
Kepler's third law ties the period to the size of the orbit in AU, and when I take the square root of the 4 AU semi-major axis, the asteroid comes out completing one orbit every 2 years.

A gravitational wave distorts spacetime inside the arms themselves, and light crossing a distorted region behaves as if it slowed down, so the detector effectively registers a change in the vacuum's refractive index.

A passing gravitational wave stretches space in one direction while squeezing it in the perpendicular one, so one arm lengthens as the other shortens, and I'd expect that mismatch to show up in the interference.
At the midpoint the field from the positive charge points away from it, toward the negative charge, and the field from the negative charge points toward itself too, so the two add in that direction.
The charges are equal and opposite, so as I work it out their pulls along the joining line balance at the midpoint, which leaves only a field pointing at right angles to that line.
If 30 percent of the 100 MJ becomes mechanical work, the other 70 percent of the chemical energy has to go somewhere, and in an engine that leftover leaves as waste heat, so I get 70 MJ.
Not all of the 70 MJ that misses becoming work leaves as heat; some goes into friction, noise and unburned fuel in the exhaust, so I'd put the heat loss itself closer to 50 MJ.
Efficiency is work divided by heat taken in, and I get the heat input by adding the 200 J of work to the 600 J exhausted, which is 800 J, so 200 over 800 gives 25 percent.
The heat taken in is the 600 J exhaust less the 200 J turned into work, leaving 400 J by my count, and 200 J of work from 400 J of input is an efficiency of 50 percent.
A wind rose shows how often the wind blows from each direction, so it tells me where emissions mostly travel and lets the protection zone stretch further downwind toward the homes most exposed.

For particulates, rain washout decides how far the dust spreads before it settles, and in a continental climate the seasonal rainfall recorded with the wind data is what I'd use to size the buffer width.

When mates are scarce, a female that ovulates only after copulation never spends yolk and energy on eggs with no chance of fertilization, and I'd say that saving matters most when encounters are rare.

Spontaneous ovulation commits a female to repeated luteal phases whether she mates or not, while ovulating only after copulation spares her from building and maintaining a corpus luteum for nothing, which I see as the saving.

The Great Filter is a step that almost no civilization gets past, and the candidate I'd point to is self-destruction through war or technology before a civilization manages to reach out across the stars.

The Great Filter says some step toward advanced life is extremely improbable, and if that step lies behind us, nobody else has passed it yet, which to me makes us the first civilization in the galaxy.
The particles are released from rest, so at that instant their velocity is zero, and with no motion under way yet I don't see any change in velocity happening, which puts the acceleration at zero.
Each particle feels the Coulomb force kq² over d² from the other, and since each has mass m, I'd apply Newton's second law and divide that force by m to get the acceleration of either one.
Climate sensitivity is defined as the warming per doubling of CO2, and the question hands me that figure directly as 1.2°C, so the feedback changes how we get there but not the sensitivity itself.
The blackbody response to doubled CO2 is 1.2°C, and the question says the water vapor feedback doubles the temperature response, so I multiply 1.2 by two and get an effective sensitivity of 2.4°C.
